proposed_node.title: Cytochrome c release triggers in apoptosis
proposed_node.canonical_question: What triggers the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondrion during apoptosis?
proposed_node.summary: Pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins (BAX, BAK) are activated by upstream death signals, oligomerise in the outer mitochondrial membrane, and form pores that release cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. Cristae remodelling first mobilises the cytochrome c pool from the crista lumen into the intermembrane space.

core.title: Cytochrome c release triggers in apoptosis

sections.heading: Two roles for cytochrome c
sections.body: Inside a healthy mitochondrion, cytochrome c has one job: carry electrons from Complex III to Complex IV in the electron transport chain. But when a cell receives a strong signal to die, cytochrome c takes on a second, very different role. It escapes from the mitochondrion into the cytoplasm, where it triggers the final stages of programmed cell death (apoptosis). Understanding how it gets out requires looking at both the outer membrane and the inner membrane folds called cristae.

sections.heading: The BCL-2 family: gatekeepers of the outer membrane
sections.body: The outer mitochondrial membrane is guarded by a family of proteins named after the first one discovered, BCL-2. Members of this family take opposite sides. Anti-apoptotic members (BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL-1) act like locks: they keep the outer membrane sealed. Pro-apoptotic effector proteins (BAX and BAK) are the potential pore-formers. In healthy cells, anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins hold BAX and BAK in check. BAX sits mostly in the cytoplasm in an inactive form; BAK is embedded in the outer membrane but held inactive by anti-apoptotic partners.

sections.heading: Death signals tip the balance
sections.body: Apoptotic signals — such as DNA damage beyond repair, loss of survival growth factors, or ER stress — activate a third group of BCL-2 proteins called BH3-only proteins (examples: BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD). BH3-only proteins act upstream. They work in two ways: some directly contact BAX and BAK and switch them on; others bind and neutralise the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins, freeing BAX and BAK to act. When enough BH3-only activity accumulates, the balance tips decisively toward cell death.

sections.heading: BAX/BAK oligomers punch holes in the outer membrane
sections.body: Once activated, BAX changes shape, inserts its hydrophobic helix into the outer mitochondrial membrane, and clusters together with BAK. Multiple BAX and BAK molecules assemble into large lipid-lined pores. This event is called mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, or MOMP. MOMP is generally considered the point of no return in apoptosis. Once the outer membrane is permeabilised, cytochrome c — along with other pro-death proteins such as SMAC/DIABLO and AIF — floods out of the intermembrane space into the cytoplasm.

sections.heading: Cristae remodelling releases the hidden pool
sections.body: Most cytochrome c is not sitting free in the intermembrane space; it is held inside the narrow folds of the inner membrane called cristae. A protein called OPA1 forms oligomeric rings that pinch the openings of cristae shut, trapping cytochrome c inside. Early in apoptosis, before MOMP is complete, OPA1 oligomers disassemble. The crista junctions open, and the large pool of cytochrome c trapped inside the cristae floods into the wider intermembrane space. This step amplifies the amount of cytochrome c available to exit once BAX/BAK pores form.

sections.heading: What happens once cytochrome c reaches the cytoplasm
sections.body: In the cytoplasm, cytochrome c binds to a scaffold protein called APAF-1. This binding causes APAF-1 to change shape and recruit several molecules of an inactive protease called procaspase-9. The resulting wheel-shaped complex is called the apoptosome. The apoptosome activates caspase-9, which in turn cleaves and activates executioner caspases (caspase-3 and caspase-7). These executioner caspases dismantle the cell in an orderly way — cutting structural proteins, activating DNA fragmentation enzymes, and packaging the contents into small membrane-bound vesicles that neighbouring cells can engulf without triggering inflammation.

sections.heading: The trigger in brief
sections.body: Cytochrome c release is not a single event but a cascade. Death signals activate BH3-only proteins, which tip the BCL-2 balance toward BAX/BAK activation. BAX and BAK oligomerise and perforate the outer membrane (MOMP). Simultaneously, OPA1 disassembly opens crista junctions to mobilise the full cytochrome c pool. Together, these two membrane events ensure that enough cytochrome c exits the mitochondrion to reliably activate the apoptosome and commit the cell to death.
